lesson.title: Evolution by Coin Flip: Understanding Genetic Drift
lesson.summary: Genetic drift is random, chance driven change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next, and its effects are strongest exactly where the Hardy-Weinberg assumption of a very large population fails hardest: in small populations.
lesson.body:
Genetic drift is the change in a population's allele frequencies that happens purely by chance, rather than because one allele confers any survival or reproductive advantage over another. It is what is left over once the Hardy-Weinberg assumption of an extremely large, effectively infinite population size breaks down. In a truly infinite population, random chance events average out perfectly and allele frequencies stay put from one generation to the next. Real populations are finite, and the smaller they are, the more the luck of which individuals happen to survive, mate, and pass on their alleles can swing frequencies up or down for no adaptive reason at all.

A useful way to picture drift is sampling error. Flip a fair coin four times and getting three heads and one tail, 75 percent heads, is not unusual at all, even though the true underlying probability is 50 percent. Flip that same coin four thousand times, and landing anywhere near 75 percent heads becomes essentially impossible, because the large sample averages the noise away. Populations behave the same way. Each new generation is, genetically speaking, a sample of gametes drawn from the parent generation. In a population of a few dozen individuals, that sample is small, so which alleles happen to get passed on can deviate substantially from the parents' true allele frequencies purely by chance. In a population of a few hundred thousand, the same random ups and downs are still occurring, but they wash out in the average.

This connects directly to variation in populations: drift acts on whatever genetic variation already exists, and over time it tends to erode that variation rather than create it. Given enough generations, drift can push an allele's frequency all the way to 100 percent, called fixation, or all the way to zero, meaning the allele is lost from the population entirely, regardless of whether that allele was helpful, harmful, or neutral. This is a critical contrast with natural selection: selection changes allele frequencies in a direction tied to fitness, while drift changes them in a direction tied to nothing but chance. Both processes can act on the same population at the same time, but drift's signature is that it can just as easily eliminate a beneficial allele or fix a mildly harmful one, something selection alone would not do.

Two specific, well documented situations make genetic drift especially powerful, and each has earned its own name because each arises from a distinct kind of event: a new population being founded by only a handful of individuals, and an existing population suddenly crashing in size. Both are really the same underlying phenomenon, drift acting hard on a small population, but the circumstances that produce the small population differ enough, and occur often enough in nature, to be worth studying separately. The next two sections take each one in turn.
